content_voiceover: This slide summarizes a British Journal of Haematology paper on the frequency and prognostic value of unconventional, meaning non-classic, genetic subtypes in pediatric and young adult B-cell precursor ALL in Taiwan. Among the unconventional subtypes, BCR-ABL1-like, also called Ph-like, is the most common, accounting for 67.3 percent of unconventional cases in children and an even higher 78.6 percent in young adults, or adolescents. There are also notable age-related differences in the underlying genetic drivers, CRLF2 rearrangement is more common in children, whereas IL7R mutations are more common in the adolescent and young adult group. Interestingly, this Taiwanese cohort had a lower overall incidence of BCR-ABL1-like disease compared to some Western cohorts, and PAX5alt subtype patients in Taiwan had a relatively better prognosis than reported elsewhere. Looking at prognosis by subtype in children, DUX4 rearranged and PAX5alt cases had favorable outcomes, while BCR-ABL1-like and MEF2D rearranged cases had poor outcomes, and both BCR-ABL1-like and MEF2D rearrangement were independent adverse prognostic factors on multivariate analysis. In adolescents and young adults, the pattern shifted, most unconventional subtypes were associated with poor prognosis in this age group, with DUX4 rearrangement being the notable exception that retained a favorable outcome.
keypoints: BCR-ABL1-like or Ph-like is the most common unconventional B-ALL subtype, 67.3% in children and 78.6% in adolescents and young adults
CRLF2 rearrangement predominates in children while IL7R mutation predominates in adolescents and young adults
In children, DUX4-R and PAX5alt predict favorable prognosis while BCR-ABL1-like and MEF2D-R are independent poor prognostic factors
In adolescents and young adults, most unconventional subtypes carry poor prognosis except DUX4-R which remains favorable
keypoint_voiceover: Key boards takeaway, BCR-ABL1-like or Ph-like ALL is the dominant unconventional subtype at all ages. DUX4 rearrangement is consistently a favorable marker in both children and young adults, while BCR-ABL1-like and MEF2D rearrangement are independent adverse prognostic factors, particularly emphasized in the pediatric group.
